newsitem.title: NEPAL: Nepali ministers said quitting in cabinet row.
newsitem.headline: Nepali ministers said quitting in cabinet row.

text.p: One Nepali minister said he had quit the fragile government and three others were reported on Sunday to have done the same to force Prime Minister Sher Bahadur Deuba's to trim the 47-member cabinet.
Minister for Parliamentary Affairs Narahari Acharya said he had resigned on Friday from the 17-month old centre-right coalition that replaced the communist government in September 1995.
"I have resigned, but I cannot say about the others," Acharya told reporters on Saturday.

Officials said Deuba, who heads a coalition of three sharply divided parties, is under pressure from his own Nepali Congress party to reduce the size of his cabinet to improve the sagging image of the party.
The Kantipur newspaper said three more ministers had resigned to put pressure on Deuba to reduce the size of his cabinet.
The newspaper identified the three ministers who quit as Home (Interior) Minister Khum Bahadur Khadga, Health Minister Arjun Narsing and Education Minister Govind Raj Joshi.
There was no independent confirmation of the report.
The four ministers who resigned belong to Deuba's Nepali Congress.
Deuba narrowly survived a communist-led no-confidence motion last December after some deputies of his coalition split and joined with the communist opposition.
He inducted some dissident deputies into the government last month and justified the size as a compulsion to keep the allies together.
Deuba's Nepal Congress party has criticised him for conceding too much to the junior coalition partners.
Officials said the prime minister was expected to seek a confidence vote in the parliament when it meets for its regular winter session next week.
Some lawmakers from Deuba's own party have openly demanded that he reduce the size of the cabinet before seeking the vote.
On paper, Deuba commands at least 105 majority in the 205 member House of Representatives, the lower house of parliament.
But the constituents of the coalition are sharply divided over whether to continue to support him.
